title: WHAT JESUS REALLY MEANT WHEN HE SAID, “THE FIRST WILL BE LAST”
paragraphs:
WHAT JESUS REALLY MEANT WHEN HE SAID, “THE FIRST WILL BE LAST”
The terrifying warning—and breathtaking hope—hidden inside one of Jesus’ most misunderstood statements
There is a sentence Jesus spoke that should make successful people uncomfortable...
and exhausted people lift their heads.
It should disturb the Christian who secretly keeps score.
It should give hope to the believer who feels forgotten.
It should confront the person who has spent years building an impressive religious life while quietly asking God, “Surely all of this means I deserve something.”
And it should reach the person reading this who feels as though everybody else got ahead while you were simply trying to survive.
Jesus said:
“Many who are first will be last, and the last first.”
In the Greek of Mark 10:31:
Πολλοὶ δὲ ἔσονται πρῶτοι ἔσχατοι καὶ οἱ ἔσχατοι πρῶτοι.
Polloi de esontai prōtoi eschatoi kai hoi eschatoi prōtoi.
Literally, the words revolve around two startling opposites:
πρῶτοι — prōtoi — first.
ἔσχατοι — eschatoi — last.
First.
Last.
Last.
First.
Jesus turns the order upside down in a single sentence.
But if you have ever heard those words reduced to “the underdog eventually wins,” you have not yet felt their full weight.
Jesus was not offering a motivational slogan about late bloomers.
He was exposing the way human beings measure greatness, goodness, sacrifice, status, reward—and even salvation itself.
And the story surrounding those words makes them almost impossible to escape.
A man came running to Jesus.
Not crawling.
Not mocking.
Running.
He knelt before Him.
He asked about eternal life.
From the outside, he looked like the kind of man religious people would have wanted sitting in the front row.
Moral.
Serious.
Respectful.
Successful.
Apparently disciplined.
And wealthy.
When Jesus reminded him of God's commandments, the man said that he had kept them from his youth.
Then Mark records one of the most beautiful details in the entire encounter.
Jesus looked at him...
and loved him.
Do not rush past that.
Before Jesus exposed his idol, Jesus loved him.
Before Jesus put His finger on the place the man did not want touched, Jesus loved him.
Before the man's sorrowful departure, Jesus loved him.
That matters because biblical conviction is not Jesus trying to destroy you.
Sometimes His love is precisely why He refuses to leave your idols unnamed.
Then came the sentence that opened the man's heart like a surgeon's blade.
One thing was lacking.
Sell what you have.
Give to the poor.
Treasure will be waiting in heaven.
Then...
“Come, follow Me.”
The tragedy is not simply that the man possessed wealth.
The tragedy is that when Jesus stood on one side and his possessions stood on the other, he could not let go.
He walked away grieving.
Imagine that scene.
He came running.
He left sorrowful.
He came asking about eternal life.
He left holding the very thing that revealed what ruled his heart.
He knelt before Jesus...
but he could not surrender to Jesus.
And suddenly this story becomes painfully modern.
Because you do not need to be wealthy to understand him.
Some people cannot surrender money.
Others cannot surrender an image.
A relationship.
A secret sin.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Control.
Recognition.
A career.
A dream.
A reputation.
A ministry.
A political identity.
The need to be admired.
The need to win every argument.
The need for people to think you are spiritually stronger than you really are.
You can kneel physically while something else still occupies the throne internally.
You can know Christian vocabulary and still protect the one room of your heart where Jesus is not allowed to rearrange the furniture.
You can sing, “I surrender all,” while quietly adding...
“except this.”
And perhaps that is why this encounter hurts.
Because the rich man is easier to criticize when we imagine his idol as money.
It becomes much harder when we give the idol our own name.
Jesus then told His disciples how difficult it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God.
The disciples were astonished.
Jesus intensified the picture with the camel and the eye of a needle.
Then they asked the question underneath every human attempt to make ourselves acceptable before God:
Who, then, can be saved?
Jesus answered that with man it is impossible...
but not with God.
That is the Gospel hiding in plain sight.
Human beings do not climb into the kingdom by becoming impressive enough.
We do not purchase salvation.
We do not outperform our neighbors into heaven.
We do not accumulate enough morality until God owes us eternal life.
Salvation is not the trophy waiting at the finish line of human achievement.
What is impossible for fallen humanity, God accomplishes.
And ultimately He accomplishes salvation through Jesus Christ.
The Son of God came for sinners.
He lived without sin.
He went to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He rose again.
And the sinner who turns to Christ in repentance and faith does not stand before God boasting, “Look what I achieved.”
The Christian stands there amazed:
“Look what Christ has done.”
But Peter had been listening.
And Peter noticed something.
The wealthy man would not leave everything.
The disciples had.
So Peter essentially said:
Look...
we left everything.
There it is.
The scoreboard.
Maybe Peter did not intend arrogance. Maybe it was bewilderment. Maybe genuine sacrifice and a very human question were tangled together.
We left our nets.
Our homes.
Our old lives.
We followed You.
What does that mean for us?
Jesus did not deny their sacrifice.

He promised that no one who had left home, family, or fields for His sake and for the Gospel would ultimately lose by following Him. He spoke of God's provision, a new family among His people, persecution in this age, and eternal life in the age to come.
Notice the word Jesus did not hide:
persecutions.
Christian discipleship is not a prosperity contract.
Jesus did not promise His followers a pain-free road decorated with luxury because they surrendered something.
He promised that following Him is worth everything...
even when following Him costs everything.
And then He said it:
“But many who are first will be last, and the last first.”
Now the sentence lands differently.
Jesus is confronting the instinct to turn discipleship into a ranking system.
The kingdom of God does not operate according to our little ladders.
The person who appears first by earthly standards may discover that heaven was never impressed by the things earth applauded.
And the person who appears last—unnoticed, unimpressive, overlooked, poor, broken, serving without applause, repenting where nobody can see—may discover that God saw everything.
But there is another danger.
Even the “last” can become proud of being last.
We can make sacrifice another status symbol.
We can start thinking:
I suffered more.
I gave more.
I served longer.
I sacrificed more.
I have been a Christian longer.
I know more Scripture.
I pray more.
I volunteer more.
I gave up things they never gave up.
Therefore...
God owes me more.
And Jesus destroys that mathematics.
Matthew's Gospel makes the point even harder to miss.
After the statement about the first and last at the end of Matthew 19, Jesus tells a story about a landowner hiring workers for his vineyard.
Some begin early.
Others arrive later.
Some have endured the burden of the day.
Others have worked only a fraction of that time.
Yet the landowner gives the later workers the agreed daily wage as well.
The early workers become angry.
Why?
Because comparison transformed generosity into an insult.
They were content with what they had been promised...
until they saw grace given to somebody else.
Read that again.
They were content...
until grace reached someone they believed deserved less.
And suddenly the parable stops being ancient.
Because there is a frightening little Pharisee hiding inside the human heart that does not merely want grace.
It wants more grace than the other person.
We celebrate the prodigal son until God throws a party for somebody whose sins hurt us.
We preach forgiveness until Jesus forgives the person we had already sentenced in our mind.
We sing about amazing grace until grace becomes amazing for somebody we think should have suffered longer.
We love testimonies of redemption...
provided the redeemed person's past is respectable enough.
But grace cannot be grace while simultaneously being wages we believe God owes us.
Jesus concludes the vineyard parable with the same reversal:
“The last will be first, and the first last.”
This does not mean obedience is meaningless.
It does not mean faithfulness is irrelevant.
It does not mean every person receives identical responsibilities or rewards regardless of faithfulness.
And it certainly does not mean repentance is unnecessary.
It means God's kingdom cannot be reduced to human entitlement.
Nobody enters eternal life because God finally looked at their résumé and admitted He was impressed.
We need mercy.
All of us.
The lifelong church member needs mercy.
The addict walking through the doors trembling needs mercy.
The preacher needs mercy.
The prisoner needs mercy.
The respectable businessman needs mercy.
The woman carrying a past she cannot bear to discuss needs mercy.
The person baptized decades ago needs mercy.
The dying thief had nothing left to build.
No decades of ministry.
No missionary journeys.
No opportunity to repair his reputation.
No lifetime left to prove that his repentance was real through years of visible service.
He had a crucified Savior beside him...
and a desperate cry of faith.
Jesus promised him paradise.
That is scandalous grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that calls evil good.
Not grace that removes repentance.
Grace purchased at the immeasurable cost of Christ's blood.
Grace that means nobody can stand at the foot of the cross and brag about how much better they climbed there than everyone else.
Maybe you have spent your life feeling last.
Maybe nobody knows how hard you have fought simply to remain faithful.
Maybe your prayers seem unanswered.
Maybe someone younger passed you.
Someone less experienced received the opportunity.
Someone else got married.
Someone else had the child.
Someone else's ministry grew.
Someone else's business succeeded.
Someone else's testimony received applause while yours seems to be happening in a room where nobody is watching.
Maybe you have quietly asked God:
“Did You forget me?”
Listen carefully.
Jesus' words do not promise that every earthly disappointment will reverse exactly the way you want.
Christian hope is deeper than “your turn is coming.”
Sometimes your earthly turn never comes.
Some faithful Christians die unknown.
Some prayers are answered differently from what we begged for.
Some wounds remain scars until resurrection.
Some obedience receives almost no applause on earth.
But if you belong to Christ, being overlooked by the world does not mean being overlooked by God.
That changes everything.
The secret prayer matters.
The temptation you resisted when nobody would have discovered the sin matters.
The money you quietly gave matters.
The person you forgave matters.
The Gospel conversation nobody applauded matters.
The tears you cried before God matter.
The decision to keep following Jesus when your emotions were screaming at you to quit matters.
He sees.
And perhaps an even more dangerous question remains.
What if you are “first”?
What if people admire your faith?
What if you have influence?
Money?
Knowledge?
A platform?
A title?
A successful ministry?
A respected family?
Thousands of followers?
What if people quote you?
What if people call you “man of God” or “woman of God”?
Then Jesus' words are not permission to hate what God has entrusted to you.
They are a warning never to confuse stewardship with superiority.
The higher you rise, the more carefully you should remember who put breath in your lungs.
Who gave the ability.
Who opened the door.
Who provided the opportunity.
Who forgave your sins.
Who carried you when nobody knew you were falling apart.
Who saved you.
Jesus.
Always Jesus.
Because Christianity is not the story of good people becoming slightly better.
It is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to a holy God through Jesus Christ.
At the cross, the world's definitions of first and last collapse completely.
Look at Jesus.
Rejected.
Mocked.
Stripped.
Beaten.
Crowned with thorns.
Crucified between criminals.
To the watching world, He looked defeated.
Last.
Finished.
A scandal hanging on Roman timber.
But death could not hold Him.
The stone moved.
The tomb emptied.
Christ rose.
And the One men rejected is Lord.
This is the kingdom's great reversal.
The King became the suffering Servant.
The innocent One stood where the guilty belonged.
The sinless One bore the judgment sinners deserved.
And those who come to Him empty-handed receive what they could never earn.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
Adoption.
New life.
Hope.
A future resurrection.
Eternal life with Christ.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
So maybe the question is no longer:
“Am I first?”
Maybe it is not even:
“Am I last?”
Maybe the question is:
Do I belong to Jesus?
Because you can be first in the world and lost.
You can be last in the world and belong to the King.
You can have everything people spend their lives chasing and still discover that none of it could save you.
And you can come to Christ with a shattered history, empty hands, a ruined reputation, tears running down your face, and nothing impressive left to offer...
and discover that grace was never waiting for you to become impressive.
It was calling you to surrender.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Stop hiding behind your achievements.
Stop hiding behind your failures.
Stop telling yourself you are too good to need saving.
Stop telling yourself you are too ruined to be saved.
Both lies keep your eyes on you.
Look at Christ.
Talk to Jesus.
Tell Him the truth.
If there is sin, confess it.
If there is pride, surrender it.
If there is bitterness, bring it into His light.
If you have been trying to earn what only grace can give, stop negotiating and come empty-handed.
And if you have never truly trusted Christ, do not confuse knowing Christian language with knowing Jesus.
Turn to Him.
He is not asking you to clean yourself sufficiently so you can become worthy of the cross.
The cross is precisely where unworthy sinners discover how astonishing the mercy of God really is.
And if this exposed something hidden in you, be brave enough to say it.
You do not have to explain the whole battle.
Sometimes two honest words are the beginning of somebody finally stepping out of hiding.
And read the other comments too.
Someone there may need to know they are not the only believer still fighting.
We are saved by grace, not by supporting a page.
But if Gospel Warrior is helping you know Christ, understand Scripture, call sin what Scripture calls it, and keep your eyes on the Gospel, you can help sustain and extend this work.
One practical way to glorify God is to steward what He has given you toward making Christ known.
But the deepest reason to stay is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
But please remember this after the link disappears from your screen.
Your sharing cannot save you.
Your religious accomplishments cannot save you.
Being first cannot save you.
Being last cannot save you.
Jesus saves.
So when the world tells you to climb higher, become louder, outrun everyone, prove yourself, collect applause, protect your position, and make certain nobody gets ahead of you...
remember the words of the King.
The first may become last.
The last may become first.
And at the end of everything, the greatest question will never be how impressive you looked standing in line.
It will be whether you belonged to the One standing at the center of eternity.
One day every scoreboard you spent your life watching will disappear—and only what Christ says about you will matter.
